chapters.title: Introduction: The Greatest Show On Earth
chapters.sourcePressure: Money decisions are shaped by identity, memory, ego, incentives, and habit before they become spreadsheet problems.
chapters.coreMove: See money as a lived behavior system before reaching for formulas.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating money as pure math, as if better information automatically creates better behavior.

chapters.title: No One's Crazy
chapters.sourcePressure: Different financial histories make risk, reward, and fear feel different, so behavior that looks irrational from outside can be coherent from inside.
chapters.coreMove: Translate a strange money choice back into the life that made it feel sensible.
chapters.commonMisread: Explaining every disagreement as stupidity, ignorance, or lack of discipline.

chapters.title: Luck & Risk
chapters.sourcePressure: Luck and risk are twin forces that can make similar processes end in praise or blame depending on the final score.
chapters.coreMove: Separate visible outcomes from the hidden mix of skill, luck, and exposure behind them.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning winners into geniuses and losers into fools based only on the scoreboard.

chapters.title: Never Enough
chapters.sourcePressure: Status competition and rising baselines can keep moving the finish line until success turns into self-destruction.
chapters.coreMove: Set the point where more stops serving the life you are trying to protect.
chapters.commonMisread: Reading enough as laziness, low ambition, or anti-growth thinking.

chapters.title: Confounding Compounding
chapters.sourcePressure: Compounding is hard to grasp because duration matters more than brilliance and results look absurd only after enough time passes.
chapters.coreMove: Protect uninterrupted time so small advantages can become large without drama.
chapters.commonMisread: Presenting compounding as a magic trick or a get-rich formula.

chapters.title: Getting Wealthy vs. Staying Wealthy
chapters.sourcePressure: Getting wealthy may reward boldness, but keeping wealth depends on endurance, restraint, and enough margin to survive shocks.
chapters.coreMove: Choose survival over brilliance when one bad break can end the game.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating wealth-building and wealth-preservation as the same skill.

chapters.title: Tails, You Win
chapters.sourcePressure: In lumpy systems, a few outsized outcomes drive most results, so average stretches and many misses are part of the structure.
chapters.coreMove: Arrange your behavior so rare big winners can matter while ordinary misses stay survivable.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming every choice must work or the strategy is broken.

chapters.title: Freedom
chapters.sourcePressure: The highest return from money is autonomy: less coercion over calendar, attention, relationships, and decisions.
chapters.coreMove: Measure money by how much control it buys over ordinary time.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing freedom to retirement fantasies or luxury leisure.

chapters.title: Man in the Car Paradox
chapters.sourcePressure: Status objects often make observers imagine themselves in the object rather than admire the owner.
chapters.coreMove: Notice when a purchase is asking strangers to admire you and redirect the money toward a value you can actually feel.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating this as a simple warning against nice things.

chapters.title: Wealth Is What You Don't See
chapters.sourcePressure: Real wealth is unspent optionality, but outsiders mostly see income and consumption.
chapters.coreMove: Train yourself to respect invisible reserves more than visible spending.
chapters.commonMisread: Equating wealth with high income or impressive possessions.

chapters.title: Save Money
chapters.sourcePressure: Saving creates options, lowers desperation, and buys time before it funds any named purchase.
chapters.coreMove: Convert ego-driven spending gaps into flexibility before life demands it.
chapters.commonMisread: Making saving only about deprivation or a future shopping goal.

chapters.title: Reasonable > Rational
chapters.sourcePressure: A money strategy must fit temperament, sleep, attention, and panic limits or its theoretical efficiency will not matter.
chapters.coreMove: Prefer the plan you can keep through fear over the plan that wins only on paper.
chapters.commonMisread: Mistaking optimization for usefulness.

chapters.title: Surprise!
chapters.sourcePressure: History is often steered by shocks, and recent calm makes people underestimate what has not happened lately.
chapters.coreMove: Build plans that expect the future to contain events your evidence cannot name yet.
chapters.commonMisread: Using history as a script for precise prediction.

chapters.title: Room for Error
chapters.sourcePressure: Margin is not waste. It lets a plan survive volatility, mistakes, tight assumptions, and bad timing.
chapters.coreMove: Pay for slack before pressure turns a small miss into forced action.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating room for error as pessimism or inefficiency.

chapters.title: You'll Change
chapters.sourcePressure: People underestimate future identity drift and can trap their later selves inside commitments made by an earlier self.
chapters.coreMove: Make long commitments with exits that respect the person you may become.
chapters.commonMisread: Using change as an excuse to avoid commitment at all.

chapters.title: Nothing's Free
chapters.sourcePressure: Good returns charge a price, often volatility, discomfort, doubt, and regret rather than an explicit invoice.
chapters.coreMove: Name the emotional fee before you buy the return.
chapters.commonMisread: Acting as if fees only mean visible charges or fund expenses.

chapters.title: You & Me
chapters.sourcePressure: Financial behavior can be rational for one horizon and costly for another; advice travels badly across different incentives.
chapters.coreMove: Identify your own game before copying someone else's signal.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming one smart person's move is automatically transferable.

chapters.title: The Seduction of Pessimism
chapters.sourcePressure: Pessimism sounds smart because threats are immediate and legible while progress is gradual and easy to miss.
chapters.coreMove: Give vivid danger its due without letting it outrank slow progress by default.
chapters.commonMisread: Replacing optimism with denial or pessimism with intelligence.

chapters.title: When You'll Believe Anything
chapters.sourcePressure: People crave tidy narratives when markets and life are random, complex, and uncertain.
chapters.coreMove: Leave messy outcomes partly unexplained instead of rushing into a neat story.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating a confident explanation as proof that the explanation is true.

chapters.title: All Together Now
chapters.sourcePressure: The strongest advice works as a system: margin protects patience, savings protect freedom, enough protects judgment.
chapters.coreMove: Combine humility, savings, patience, and enough into one repeatable temperament.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the recap into a generic list of tips.

chapters.title: Confessions
chapters.sourcePressure: Broad truths still need private weighting across independence, simplicity, cash, risk, and ambition.
chapters.coreMove: Translate durable principles into a personal plan you can defend without pretending it is universal.
chapters.commonMisread: Reading personal confession as permission to ignore principles.

chapters.title: Postscript: A Brief History of Why the U.S. Consumer Thinks the Way They Do
chapters.sourcePressure: Postwar U.S. policy, housing, rates, demobilization, borrowing, and consumer demand shaped behaviors that later felt normal.
chapters.coreMove: Treat today's money defaults as historical inheritances rather than neutral common sense.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning history into trivia instead of using it to question defaults.
